topic: Netgear countersues TP-Link over 'Chinese company' rebrand
headline_marked: Netgear [[accuses TP-Link of false advertising]] over 'American company' rebrand, citing Chinese ties
headline: Netgear accuses TP-Link of false advertising over 'American company' rebrand, citing Chinese ties
summary: Netgear's federal court filing alleges TP-Link's 2024 reincorporation as a California company deceptively hides ongoing R&D and manufacturing in China, following a DoD designation.
details: Netgear has filed counterclaims against TP-Link in federal court, accusing its rival of false advertising. The suit alleges TP-Link's 2024 reincorporation as a California company is a deception, concealing significant R&D and manufacturing operations in China. This move follows the U.S. DoD adding TP-Link Technologies to its list of Chinese military companies.

The counterclaims respond to a lawsuit TP-Link initiated last November, which accused Netgear of a smear campaign. TP-Link alleged Netgear's CEO falsely linked it to cyberattacks and breached a 2024 settlement where TP-Link paid Netgear $135 million. Parts of TP-Link's original case based on third-party statements have since been dismissed.

Netgear denies the smear allegations and is now on the offensive, bringing four counterclaims under various trade-practice laws. It specifically targets TP-Link's claim of having entirely split from China-based TP-Link Technologies to operate as an independent American company. Netgear argues this statement misleads consumers.

According to Netgear's filing, TP-Link Technologies did not fundamentally reorganize its global operations. Instead, it allegedly changed its name to Lianzhou but continues to perform much of TP-Link’s R&D and manufacturing in China under the same co-founder. Netgear states TP-Link employed over 13,000 people in China through 2024, including 9,000 in manufacturing, compared to about 350 U.S. employees.

The filing also challenges TP-Link's "Made in Vietnam" labeling as misleading. Netgear claims the Vietnamese plant primarily serves as a final assembly point, with 99.5% of components for U.S.-bound products imported from China. This comes amid an FCC import ban on routers not built in the U.S.

Netgear's counterclaim heavily references the DoD’s designation of TP-Link Technologies as "directly affiliated with the PLA" and a contributor to China’s defense industrial base. Netgear asserts that "TP-Link remains, at its core, a Chinese company selling Chinese-made products."

TP-Link rejects these premises, maintaining it is a U.S.-headquartered company not subject to foreign government control. It also asserts that its products are genuinely made in Vietnam. The companies also dispute their commercial market share, with Netgear claiming TP-Link holds roughly 65% of the U.S. retail router market, while TP-Link states its share is under 10%.

This legal battle is unfolding alongside broader federal scrutiny of TP-Link from various U.S. agencies, including Commerce, the FCC, the FTC, and state attorneys general in Texas and Florida. The outcome could have significant implications for the router market and supply chain transparency.

topic: AI OSS tool repo archived after $7.3M Seed funding
headline_marked: [[TensorZero's AI OSS repo archived]] overnight after raising $7.3M seed funding
headline: TensorZero's AI OSS repo archived overnight after raising $7.3M seed funding
summary: TensorZero, an open-source LLMOps platform used by Fortune 10 companies and powering ~1% of global LLM API spend, has unexpectedly archived its public repository.
details: TensorZero, an open-source LLMOps platform that recently secured $7.3 million in seed funding, has abruptly archived its public GitHub repository. This unexpected move comes despite the platform's significant adoption, powering approximately 1% of global LLM API spend.

The platform offered a 100% self-hosted solution for LLM observability, prompt optimization, and A/B testing. It integrated seamlessly with major LLM providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google AI Studio, supporting any OpenAI-compatible API.

Alongside the open-source core, TensorZero offered 'Autopilot,' a complementary paid product for automated AI engineering. The team comprised former Rust compiler maintainers and machine learning researchers from top universities, backed by investors in leading open-source projects and AI labs.

TensorZero was utilized by companies ranging from frontier AI startups to Fortune 10 enterprises. Its quick start guide promised a production-ready LLM application with observability and fine-tuning in just five minutes.

The archiving of the repository means the open-source code is no longer publicly accessible or maintained. This leaves users and companies relying on the platform to seek alternatives or manage existing deployments without official updates.
